1nvip0g:252: Efficiency optimization for general LLMs mainly relies on model scale (more parameters, fewer tokens) and quantization strategies. But remote sensing models face structured high-dimensional tensors [H, W, T, D=12], and their efficiency bottleneck has a unique structure—it lies not in semantic compression of tokens, but in token redundancy along spatial and temporal dimensions. SatMAE proved that "resolution-separated tokens" work, and CROMA proved that "single token, all bands" also works. Both approaches working suggests that token design for remote sensing data is still unsettled. v1.1 finds a new balance between the two—merging resolution tokens while modifying the pretraining strategy.

8fjjib:227: Transformer computational complexity grows as O(n²) with token sequence length, one of the core bottlenecks for applying LLMs to remote sensing. When processing satellite imagery covering 100,000 square kilometers, even if each patch produces only a few dozen tokens, the accumulated sequence length makes inference costs unacceptably high. v1.1 reduces token count to 1/3, meaning O(n²) becomes O((n/3)²)—computation drops to roughly 1/9 of the original. This is not marginal optimization; it changes the fundamental judgment of "what geographic scale is economically feasible."

f1yqm1:190: OlmoEarth v1.1 is trained on exactly the same dataset as v1, changing only the pretraining methodology. This design is extremely rare in remote sensing pretraining research—most papers change architecture, dataset, and algorithm simultaneously, making results impossible to attribute. v1.1's approach makes the performance difference between the two versions point precisely to the effect of the token merging strategy. This approach is worth adopting by other researchers in remote sensing: when evaluation metrics are affected by multiple variables, fixing the dataset and isolating the methodology variable first is necessary to build reliable scientific understanding.
f5x1c1:256: OlmoEarth v1.1's efficiency breakthrough comes not from architectural restructuring but from fine-tuning the data encoding strategy—merging Sentinel-2's 3 resolution tokens into 1, directly cutting token count by 2/3. But this operation has an engineering cost: naive merging causes a 10-percentage-point performance regression, showing that modeling spatial relationships between bands is critical for remote sensing tasks. The team compensated for this loss by modifying the pretraining strategy, ultimately achieving the dual goal of "3x efficiency + comparable performance." This case shows that on large Transformer models, fine-grained data encoding design is often a higher-leverage optimization than architectural innovation.
